strengths: The task is practically motivated: a reference photograph and a relative description provide complementary information for retrieving people across appearance changes. SynCPR’s 1.15 million synthetic triplets and ITCPR’s 2,202 queries against 20,510 gallery images could provide useful community resources.

Generating both person views within one image is a sensible identity-consistency heuristic. Combining this with bidirectional captions, LoRA adaptation, and multimodal filtering forms a coherent data-construction pipeline.

Table 1 includes meaningful comparisons using the same training dataset. Training SPRC on SynCPR raises Rank-1 from 25.07% to 42.27%; FAFA further reaches 46.54%, with mAP improving from 51.62% to 55.60%. These results support contributions from both the dataset and retrieval method.

The component ablations and additional CIRR experiment strengthen the empirical case. On CIRR, FAFA achieves 54.48% Rank-1 versus SPRC’s 51.96%. The manuscript is generally well organized, with helpful diagrams, generation prompts, and substantial training details.
weaknesses: The principal concern is evaluation independence. Section 4.3 and Appendix C.4 appear to select the filtering threshold, alpha, k, auxiliary-loss weights, and masking ratio using ITCPR performance. Yet Appendix B.1.3 designates ITCPR exclusively for testing, and no separate validation protocol is described. Adapting both dataset construction and model settings to the only CPR test benchmark risks optimistic results. An untouched evaluation is needed to establish the main performance claims reliably.

The central dataset-quality claims exceed the evidence. Joint generation encourages identity consistency but does not ensure it, and averaging four MLLM scores can conceal a poor identity-consistency score. No independent human audit reports identity errors, caption correctness, or agreement with the automatic evaluator. ITCPR similarly lacks annotation-agreement and residual false-negative estimates; inspecting encoder-retrieved neighbors does not establish complete relevance labeling.

Experimental attribution remains incomplete. LoRA adaptation and joint versus independent image generation receive qualitative comparisons without controlled downstream ablations. FDA simultaneously changes feature aggregation, distribution matching, and group-based labels, so Table 2 does not isolate their contributions. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported, which particularly matters for the incremental MFR improvement of 0.49 Rank-1 points and 0.11 mAP points over FDA plus FD.

Originality needs sharper positioning. FAFA builds on BLIP-2’s query representations and established matching, diversity, and reconstruction objectives. The relationship to existing query-based similarity aggregation is insufficiently explained. Prior CIR data-construction approaches such as CASE and CompoDiff appear in the appendix comparisons but receive little substantive discussion against the proposed synthesis pipeline.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendix. The MFR decoder architecture, exact FLUX modules receiving LoRA, and batch-sampling strategy for same-GID partial positives are unspecified. The latter directly affects the proposed soft-label objective. The text also alternates between Qwen2.5-70B and 72B, and provides no synthesis GPU-hour accounting. Code and data release is promised rather than demonstrated in the manuscript.

The claims of comprehensive ethnic representation and the privacy motivation need qualification. Demographic coverage is not quantified, and the generator is adapted using real person images while the benchmark reuses identifiable people. Source-data reuse permissions and implications for privacy are not discussed. These are documentation gaps rather than evidence of misconduct; the evaluation and dataset-validation shortcomings primarily determine the rejection.
